name: Chinese kunqu opera
lineage: Chinese kunqu opera. Kunqu crystallized in the Kunshan region (south of Suzhou, Jiangsu province) during the late Ming dynasty (sixteenth century) under the founding theorist-composer Wei Liangfu (c.1489-1566), who codified the kunqu-tunes system based on the older Kunshan-region folk-tune vocabulary. The genre flourished through the Ming-Qing transition as the dominant elite-class theatrical-and-musical form, with the canonical play-cycles of the Mudan Ting (Peony Pavilion, 1598, Tang Xianzu) and Changsheng Dian (Palace of Eternal Life, 1688, Hong Sheng) constituting the core repertoire. Performance integrates singing, stylized dance-movement, recited dialogue, and instrumental accompaniment in a fully-integrated theatrical form. Vocal style features wide melisma, characteristic dyhayou portamento sliding-pitch ornament, and an elaborate ornament-vocabulary tied to specific text-tones and emotion-categories. The accompanying ensemble centers on the qudi flute (the principal melodic carrier, a transverse bamboo flute), sanxian (three-string plucked lute), pipa (four-string pear-shaped plucked lute), and a percussion battery for theatrical-cue work. The mid-twentieth-century cultural-revolutionary period nearly extinguished the form; the post-1980 revival under conservatory programs and the touring company circuit has restored continuity. Yu Zhenfei (1902-1993) is among the twentieth-century canonical performers. Distinguished from later Beijing opera (jingju) by kunqu's elite-literary-elegant register and slower tempo; distinguished from Cantonese opera (yueju) by Wu-Mandarin lyric-language and Jiangnan-region cadential conventions.
